title: Hosted API demo - chat/text generation basics
summary: Redwood hosted API demo focused on chat/text generation: streaming, key parameters (temperature, top_p, max_tokens), retry/backoff behavior, and basic cost/latency tradeoffs. Customer uses OpenAI today; main concerns are latency SLOs (~300ms tail), data residency, SOC2/KMS, and predictable cost. Agreed next steps: send security docs, pricing comparison hosted vs dedicated, share benchmark script, schedule POC week of 2026-04-27.

transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2026-04-20 15:00 PT
Duration: 42 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Meyers (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Marta Ruiz (Cadenza), Daniel Kim (Cadenza), Olivia Zhang (Cadenza)

[00:00] Jordan: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I'm Jordan Meyers from Redwood Inference. With me is Priya Nair, our solutions engineer. How's everyone doing?
[00:08] Marta: Hi Jordan, hi Priya. Good, excited to see the demo. I'm Marta, head of ML at Cadenza.
[00:12] Olivia: Olivia here, CTO. We have Daniel on infra but he might hop in with questions.
[00:17] Daniel: Yep hi all.
[00:20] Jordan: Great. Quick agenda: we'll run through the hosted API for chat/text generation, show streaming, cover common parameters (temperature, top_p, max_tokens), how retries and backoff work, and then a quick look at console/observability. We'll leave time for Q&A and next steps. Sound good?
[00:30] Marta: Sounds perfect.

--- Demo start ---
[02:10] Priya: Okay jumping in, here is a simple chat example via our hosted API. I'll paste a short request. Note that the API supports streaming where you can receive partial tokens as they're generated; this is useful for UI responsiveness. You can see here we open a WebSocket/HTTP stream and get chunked tokens, so the perceived latency is a lot lower even if total generation time is the same.
[02:45] Priya: Example snippet: messages role user content "Summarize Q1 revenue for our product line"; params: temperature 0.2, max_tokens 150, top_p 0.95, n 1. For low-latency summarization we recommend low temperature and constrain max_tokens. Also we have stop sequences and function-calling if you want structured outputs.
[03:20] Marta: Quick question - how does streaming interact with prefixes and KV cache? We have a lot of multi-turn history.
[03:29] Priya: Good question. We use KV cache on the server side to keep recent context cached per session. Streaming is orthogonal - we stream generated tokens as they are produced by the model while the KV cache speeds up subsequent tokens and repeated prefixes. If you pin model versions, the cache is maintained for that model variant. Transcription note: I said K-V cache but the transcript sometimes shows K V chash, sorry.
[04:05] Daniel: For multi-tenant hosted customers, is the KV cache shared across tenants? We need strict isolation.
[04:13] Priya: No, KV cache is per-customer session and per model instance; isolation's enforced. For Dedicated/Private you get further isolation and VPC-level controls.
[04:28] Olivia: You're mentioning Dedicated - curious about the tradeoffs between hosted and dedicated for us. Our main constraints are latency SLO (~300ms p95 for short prompts), and predictable cost.
[04:40] Jordan: Right, hosted is fastest to get started, lower operational overhead; we give performance profiles for each model variant. Dedicated provides reserved GPU pools for predictable throughput and can hit lower variance for tail latency. For p95 300ms it depends on model selection and quantization - for small summarization models hosted often meets that, but large context/gen models might need Dedicated with pinned lower-latency kernels.
[05:05] Marta: Budget-wise, how do you suggest we control cost? We do a lot of embedding + chat.
[05:12] Priya: Controls: batching and prefix caching reduce per-token costs, quantization options (e.g., 4-bit) can lower compute dramatically, and our Optimize module gives recommendations per workload. Also route-by-policy allows you to send low-risk prompts to cheaper model variants.
[05:30] Daniel: About retries - if a token stream fails mid-response how does Redwood handle that? We'd rather not double-charge users or show partial duplicates.
[05:40] Priya: Retries have an idempotency key and a resume token approach. For shorter streaming failures we can resume from the last acknowledged token if the model supports caching; otherwise we do a controlled retry with exponential backoff. We also surfaced a retry header so client's UI can detect duplicate fragments and dedupe. There is also server-side retry with rate-limited backoff for transient infra errors.
[06:10] Olivia: Any hard limits for streaming sessions? We have some long-running conversations.
[06:16] Jordan: Session durations are configurable - by default we keep session KV cache for 24 hours of inactivity but that can be extended in Dedicated/Private. Max tokens per call can be set by policy.

[07:00] Priya (demo continues): Now I'll show parameter effects - temperature at 0.0 vs 0.8, top_p toggles. Notice how higher temperature increases variability; for deterministic summarization we recommend temp 0.0-0.3 and top_p 0.9-1.0. Also show using max_tokens to cap and avoid runaway generation.
[07:45] Marta: Do you have guidance for streaming QoS so the UI doesn't jitter? We saw early websockets had bursty token delivery.
[07:54] Priya: We smooth at the SDK level - you can buffer small intervals (like 50-200ms) to avoid micro-jitter. Streaming also supports chunk metadata timestamps so you can render progressively.

[09:20] Daniel: Security - SOC2, KMS for keys, and SSO integration are big for us. Do you have compliance docs?
[09:28] Jordan: Yes - we have a SOC2 Type II report, SAML SSO, RBAC in Console, and KMS/HSM integrations for Private deployments. I'll attach the security datasheet after the call.
[09:40] Olivia: Data residency - we need EU-only storage for some projects.
[09:45] Priya: Hosted supports region pinning; we have EU regions and also Private for full on-prem or VPC deployments. We can discuss data retention policies per contract.

[10:30] Marta: What about observability? We need traces per request and token-level cost breakdowns.
[10:36] Priya: Console shows per-route latency, token cost breakdown, and you can export traces to your tracing backend. We also provide request sampling and full audit logs for Dedicated/Private.

[11:50] Priya (walkthrough): Switching to a quick live code block - here's a streaming sample using fetch and EventSource.
[12:05] "fetch('/v1/generate', {method: 'POST', body: JSON.stringify({model: 'redwood-compact-1', messages: [...], stream: true, temperature: 0.2})})"
[12:18] Priya: The SDK automatically handles reconnects with backoff; if you prefer manual control you can set retry_policy: none.
[12:30] Marta: Do you support function calling for structured outputs?
[12:33] Priya: Yes, functions and tool-calls are supported. We map the model output into JSON schema and can validate. Perfect for things like invoice extraction or structured summarization.

[14:00] Daniel: Ops question: how does rate limiting work per account? We have many internal teams and want per-team quotas.
[14:07] Jordan: We expose per-token quotas and per-route quotas. You can create API keys scoped to projects and set quotas in Console. For Dedicated customers we provide quota policies per pool.

[15:40] Marta: Can we run an A/B between two model variants to compare cost & quality?
[15:45] Priya: Absolutely - rollouts in Console let you split traffic, do canary, A/B, and auto-fallback to a cheaper model if latency spikes. You can define success metrics based on evals.

[16:30] Olivia: What about offline benchmarking? We want reproducible latency numbers on our prompts.
[16:36] Priya: We'll share a benchmark script that runs synthetic and real prompt sets against hosted endpoints and returns p50/p95/p99, token cost, and resource usage. We'll also include instructions for running it from your VPC if needed.

[18:10] Jordan: Quick pause - any blockers for doing a POC? Timelines?
[18:16] Marta: We're evaluating two pilots. First is a summarization/assistant feature for our pricing tool (high volume, short responses). Second is an analytics agent that needs longer context. We want to start the first POC ASAP, ideally next week.
[18:30] Jordan: Great - we can do a hosted POC for the summarization one and then run the analytics POC on Dedicated or a mixed route depending on latency needs.

[19:00] Daniel: One more low-level question: when you mention quantization, what precision do you recommend for inference to balance quality? 8-bit? 4-bit?
[19:09] Priya: For most transformer-based summarization, 4-bit (LLM.int4 style) is often a good balance - at least for medium models. Large generation models sometimes see small quality drops; Optimize will suggest per-model quantization profiles from our evaluation runs. We'll include profile suggestions in the benchmark sheet.

[20:40] Marta: Any pitfalls we should be aware of with retries and streaming? For example double billing or duplicate responses in the UI.
[20:48] Priya: The idempotency key prevents double billing for retries of the same request. For UI duplicates, use the resume token or dedupe on the client: each chunk includes an offset so you can detect replays. We'll include sample client code.

[22:15] Priya (demo wrap-up): Last part - Console quick tour: you can view per-model latency histograms, per-route costs, and token breakdowns. Here's where you define rollouts and quotas. We also show the Optimize recommendations and recent regressions flagged by evals.
[23:10] Olivia: That looks useful. Audit logs - can we export them to our SIEM?
[23:16] Jordan: Yes, we support pushing logs to S3 or Cloud Storage and forwarding to third-party SIEMs. For Dedicated/Private customers we can set retention and export rules.

[24:50] Marta: Pricing question - how do you price streaming? Is it per-token or per-call?
[24:55] Jordan: It's per-token generated and per-token input; streaming doesn't change billing semantics. We also show cost per request in Console. For Dedicated there are reserved capacity commitments and lower per-token unit costs.

[26:10] Daniel: Around SLAs - do you have guaranteed latencies or uptime?
[26:15] Jordan: For hosted, we provide uptime SLA and best-effort latency commitments with performance profiles. Dedicated comes with stronger SLAs and optionally latency SLOs in the contract.

[28:00] Marta: Ok let's talk about next steps - we want the security pack and the benchmark script. Also can you send a suggested configuration for our summarization POC (model, params, expected cost)?
[28:10] Priya: We'll put together a one-pager: recommended model (redwood-compact-1 or redwood-medium-gen), suggested params (temp 0.2, top_p 0.95, max_tokens 120), sampling cadence, and estimated cost per 1k requests.

[29:20] Olivia: For the POC, can we have a week-long hosted run with 100k requests? We'll need a committed pricing quote for that volume.
[29:30] Jordan: Yes we can provide a pilot pricing quote. I'll include a hosted pilot and an option for a small dedicated pool if needed.

[31:00] Daniel: Minor infra item - do you support mutual TLS for private endpoints?
[31:06] Priya: For Private yes; for hosted we have TLS and customer-level auth; mutual TLS is available for Private/VPC installations.

[32:50] Marta: Any notes on model drift monitoring? We want automatic regressions detection.
[32:56] Priya: Optimize includes eval hooks and baseline prompt sets. You can run continuous evals and get alerted on regressions. We also let you pin and rollback model versions automatically.

[34:20] Jordan: Alright wrap-up: we'll send security docs + SOC2, the benchmark script and runbook, pricing for hosted pilot and dedicated option, and a recommended param/config for the summarization POC. We'll aim to get that all to you by Thu 4/22.
[34:40] Marta: Sounds great. Any final questions?
[34:45] Olivia: None from me.
[34:49] Daniel: All good.

[35:00] Jordan: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up with the docs and calendar invite for the POC kickoff next week.
[35:07] Marta: Thanks.

--- End meeting transcript (approx 42 mins) ---

Notes on transcription: occasional mis-hearings (e.g., "K V chash" for KV cache), generic speaker labels, and some run-on sentences preserved to mimic Fireflies style.
